key_idea: CURE-TSD-Real video benchmark with 12 simulated challenge types at 5 levels (rain, haze, shadow, exposure, dirty lens and others) to measure how benign conditions degrade sign detection and how this shows in spectra.
method: Controlled degradations of 49 real sequences; two benchmark detectors; magnitude spectra of residual videos correlated with detection loss.
data: CURE-TSD-Real: 49 challenge-free real sequences, 60 challenge versions of each
reported_result: Abstract: severe conditions reduce precision by 29% and recall by 68% on average. Paper text: decolorization removes all of one detector's performance, showing reliance on colour; simulated shadow causes the least degradation.
relation_to_project: All slides: labelled benign condition changes (shadow, exposure, haze) for false-alarm testing of a sign-consistency check; also warns that colour cues can fail under decolorization.

title: Traffic Sign Classifiers Under Physical World Realistic Sticker Occlusions: A Cross Analysis Study
key_idea: Studies realistic-looking stickers, both vandalism and optimised placement, on 11 sign classifiers; finds that covering the few distinctive features of a class, not salient adversarial texture, drives misclassification.
method: Sticker content matched to brightness, contrast and blur; random, structured and model-cross (MCSA) placement; cross-model transfer analysis; dashboard field tests including RP2 and AP.
data: GTSRB (43 classes); five safety-critical classes in three shapes (triangle, circle, octagon); dashboard videos of real signs
reported_result: Paper text: up to five random stickers (up to 20% coverage) gave no significant drop; MCSA cut field accuracy to near zero for four classes while the stop sign stayed at 100%, attributed to its unique octagon and STOP word.
relation_to_project: Slide 01: unique-shape classes resist sticker occlusion and benign vandalism stickers rarely flip a classifier, which bounds the benign-sticker false-alarm case; class-critical features (the digit 3 for 30 km/h) are named as checkable cues.
notes: Record read: Crossref (no abstract). Abstract and sections IV and V read from the TUM institutional copy in a search result. Fluorescent stickers were not tested (authors' note).

title: Fooling the Eyes of Autonomous Vehicles: Robust Physical Adversarial Examples Against Traffic Sign Recognition Systems
venue: Proceedings 2022 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
key_idea: Physical adversarial examples against detector-based traffic-sign recognition, with in-vehicle camera simulation and filters; four attack goals (hiding, appearance, non-target, target), tested on a production vehicle.
method: Pipeline for robust physical adversarial examples against object detectors used for TSR; simulated in-vehicle camera effects; hiding and non-target attacks run against a 2021 model-year vehicle.
data: Traffic sign detectors; field tests with a 2021 production vehicle
reported_result: Paper text read: hiding and non-target attacks fooled the TSR system of a 2021 model-year vehicle; defenses by image preprocessing, adversarial example detection and model enhancement are discussed.
relation_to_project: Slides 01 and 05: attacks reach production TSR, which is detector-based, so a check must work on detector boxes; the hiding attack (sign vanishes) is the case a shape-prior check cannot see without an earlier detection, a track or a map.
